podcast.title: Art School Background
podcast.body: Attended art school before joining Sean Penn Atenshry as the guitar player, a decision that led him to quit his studies. This background is credited by Hugh Dillon for influencing his unique and less "stereotypical" guitar style. "I was going to art school at the time. I do, I was a slightly different background than you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Childhood Friend and Musical Influence on Tim White
podcast.body: Carr has known Tim White since childhood and played a pivotal role in White's musical journey. He suggested White buy a bass instead of a guitar, and later provided White's "musical rock and roll education" by exposing him to bands like Led Zeppelin and The Who, fostering White's development as a bassist. "Trent said, no, you should get a bass. I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, okay. Yeah."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Distinctive Guitar Style
podcast.body: Hugh Dillon highlights Carr's guitar playing as non-"stereotypical dumb guitar rock," attributing its artistic quality to his art school background. Dillon finds inspiration in Carr's riffs, which he describes as subconscious musical pieces. "I think because he was an artist, it wasn't stereotypical dumb guitar rock. There was something in it that I recognized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Early Jamming Leading to The Headstones
podcast.body: As friends with Mark Gibson, Carr began jamming with Randy Kwan at a house on Carlson. Hugh Dillon later joined these sessions, creating an "electric moment" where the musical chemistry felt like a "real band" forming, which eventually became The Headstones. "Mark and Randy and I were jamming and he came in and it was just like, that was cool. Like one of those electric moments."

xref.title: Early Role in Sean Penn Atenshry
xref.body: He was initially "driving" the pre-Headstones band Sean Penn Atenshry, and jammed with Mark Gibson and Trent Carr at a house on Carlson before Hugh Dillon joined. "So it was Randy driving it and, you know, we're drinking a lot and having a lot of fun."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Hugh Dillon's Recovery Journey
xref.body: Hugh Dillon's recovery from addiction was a long and arduous process, supported primarily by his wife Midori, manager Bernie Brin, and bandmates Tim White and Trent Carr, who never gave up on him. He underwent multiple rehab and detox programs, eventually reaching a point of honesty that enabled change. "My wife, my family, my wife is the, Midori is the prime mover and all of it because she never, and like these guys, and this is why I go back to the people behind the scenes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

xref.title: Hugh's Producing Role and Band Dynamics
xref.body: As a lyricist and singer who took on a producing role, Hugh Dillon often struggled to articulate musical problems, relying on Tim White's ability to "disassemble a song" and Trent Carr's natural, "painter-like" talent, despite the frustration of trying to capture specific takes. "I'm a lyricist and a singer. I don't have the same skill set."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

xref.title: Jamming with Future Headstones Members
xref.body: Was friends with Trent Carr and began jamming with him and Randy Kwan at a house on Carlson. This early jamming group eventually evolved into The Headstones with the addition of Hugh Dillon. "Well I was friends with Mark and I was going to art school at the time... And then I was friends with Mark and we started jamming with Randy on this, at this house on uh, Carlson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Kingston Origins and Early Formation
xref.body: The core members originated from Kingston, where they were part of a vibrant music scene that also produced The Tragically Hip. The band's genesis involved a group called "Sean Penn Atenshry" in the mid-1980s, which included Hugh Dillon, Randy Kwan, Mark Gibson, and Frontini, before Trent Carr joined and transformed their sound, leading to The Headstones' formation. "So how the headstones come out of Kingston? What year are we talking about? 89? No, you came from Kingston earlier than that. It was like 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Musical Education Through Trent Carr
xref.body: With few other friends, White spent weekends at Trent Carr's downtown Toronto home, receiving his "musical rock and roll education." Carr would play him records by bands like Led Zeppelin and The Who, inspiring White to practice bass alone throughout the week. "He'd play me like, let's out on a pink floor and the who and all these bands. And then I'd go home and play bass all week by myself and then come back and show him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scarborough Upbringing
xref.body: Grew up in Scarborough, Ontario, which he characterized as a "cultural wasteland" due to a lack of local musical scene or friends outside of Trent Carr. "I grew up in Scarborough, which was a cultural wasteland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Subconscious Noodling Songwriting Method
xref.body: The band's songwriting often begins with Trent Carr or Tim White "noodling" subconsciously during live performances or jams. Hugh Dillon actively listens for these spontaneous musical ideas, isolating specific notes or riffs that he finds unique and then developing them into full songs, rather than deliberately trying to write "hits." "I'll hear them subconsciously noodle. And that's when I stop everybody and what's that?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Trent Carr's Influence on Becoming a Bassist
xref.body: Became a bass player because his childhood friend Trent Carr advised him to. When White expressed interest in buying a guitar, Carr told him he should get a bass instead, a suggestion White readily accepted. "The only reason I'm a bass player is because I was, I've known Trent since I was really young... Trent said, no, you should get a bass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Trent Carr's Post-Breakup Creative Path
xref.body: After the band's hiatus, Trent Carr focused on his artistic pursuits and began writing music for film and TV, successfully scoring the film "Giant Sub-Africa," which is available on Netflix. He preferred not to play in another band after the Headstones. "I kind of made it work in that world a little bit and then just kind of kept doing that part of it all kept my toe and being a musician but never tried to play in a band after that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
